n: Some time later Jesus crosses the Sea of Galilee. John gives its second name, Tiberias, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named for the Roman emperor.

f.g: Also called the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1) and Chinnereth in the Old Testament.

n: Crowds follow him, drawn mostly by the healings they have seen. John quietly sets up the question the chapter will press: why are people following Jesus?

f.g: John’s word is “signs” (Greek sēmeia) — miracles that point beyond themselves to who Jesus is.

n: Jesus climbs into the hill country above the lake and sits down with his disciples — the posture of a teacher in that culture.
John notes that Passover is near. That detail matters: the feast recalled manna and deliverance from Egypt, and Jesus is about to feed a multitude and call himself the true bread from heaven.
Seeing the huge crowd approaching, Jesus asks Philip where they could buy bread. Philip was from nearby Bethsaida, so the question was natural — but it was also a test.
John explains that Jesus already knew what he would do. He was inviting Philip to stretch his faith beyond what money and markets could supply.

f.g: prove = test, try out. The aim was to strengthen Philip, not trap him.

n: Philip does the math: even two hundred days’ wages would not buy enough for each person to get a bite. Human resources are plainly not enough.

f.g: Two hundred denarii. A denarius was roughly one day’s pay for a laborer, so this is about eight months’ wages.

n: Andrew, who earlier brought his brother Peter to Jesus, steps forward with what little he has found.
A boy has five barley loaves and two small fish. Barley bread was the cheap food of the poor. Andrew offers it while admitting it seems useless — yet Jesus uses small offerings.

f.g: Elisha also fed a crowd with barley loaves, and there was food left over.
Probably dried or salted fish eaten with bread, common around the lake.

n: Jesus has the people sit on the spring grass. About five thousand men are counted, besides women and children, which makes this the only miracle besides the Resurrection found in all four Gospels.

f.g: Green grass fits the spring Passover season noted in verse 4.

n: Jesus gives thanks and the food is shared until everyone has as much as they want. The actions — taking, giving thanks, distributing — echo the Last Supper and the sacrament.
Jesus tells the disciples to gather the leftovers so nothing is wasted. God’s abundance is generous, but never careless.
Twelve baskets of leftovers are collected — far more than the five loaves they began with. Some see the number twelve as a hint that Jesus can feed all the tribes of Israel.

f.g: Greek kophinos — a sturdy wicker basket travelers carried.

n: The crowd concludes Jesus must be “that prophet” Moses promised — a new Moses who, like the first, provides bread in the wilderness.

f.w: that prophet that should come into the world

n: Realizing they intend to force him to be their king, Jesus slips away alone into the hills. He would not become the political, bread-giving deliverer they wanted.

f.g: Matthew and Mark add that he went up to pray.

n: As evening falls the disciples go down to the shore without him.

f.g: even = evening.

n: They set out by boat across the lake toward Capernaum. It is now dark and Jesus has not joined them — a scene of being alone and in the dark.

f.g: A fishing town on the north shore that served as Jesus’s home base in Galilee.

n: A strong wind stirs up the water. The Sea of Galilee sits low among hills, and sudden storms still sweep down on it.
After rowing about three or four miles, they see Jesus walking on the water toward them and are terrified.

f.w: five and twenty or thirty furlongs
f.g: A furlong (Greek stadion) was about 600 feet, so 25–30 furlongs is roughly 3 to 3½ miles.

n: Jesus calms them: “It is I; don’t be afraid.” In Greek his words are literally “I am” — an echo of the divine name that John will develop throughout this Gospel.

f.g: Greek egō eimi, “I am.”

n: Gladly they take him aboard, and right away the boat reaches shore. John lets the abrupt arrival hint at more power at work.

f.w: immediately the ship was at the land

n: The next day the crowd on the far shore puzzle over Jesus: there had been only one boat, and he had not gotten into it with the disciples.

f.g: John includes these details to show the crowd could not explain how Jesus had crossed.

n: In a side note, John explains that other boats had come over from Tiberias, near the place of the feeding — which is how the crowd could follow.

f.w: after that the Lord had given thanks
f.g: John again highlights the thanksgiving, as if it were the heart of the meal.

n: Unable to find Jesus or his disciples, the people board boats and sail to Capernaum to look for him.

f.g: Seeking Jesus is good — but the next verses ask why they are seeking him.

n: Finding him, they call him “Rabbi” and ask when he arrived. They want an explanation of the crossing; Jesus will answer a deeper question instead.

f.g: Rabbi = “my teacher,” a respectful title.

n: Jesus gently exposes their motive: they came back not because the miracle pointed them to God but because they got a free meal.

f.g: Greek amēn, amēn — “truly, truly.” John alone records Jesus doubling it for solemn emphasis.

n: Don’t spend your life working for food that spoils, Jesus says; seek the food that lasts forever, which he will give. The Father has put his seal of approval on him.

f.g: meat = food in general, not only flesh.
Like a seal stamped on a document — the Father has authenticated and authorized his Son.

n: Picking up his word “labour,” the crowd ask what works they must do to please God, expecting a list of duties.
Jesus answers that the essential “work” God asks is to believe in the One he has sent. Real faith in Christ is where all righteous works begin.

f.w: believe on him whom he hath sent

n: Astonishingly, the same people who were fed the day before ask for a sign to prove Jesus’s claim.

f.g: shewest = showest.

n: They hint at the sign they want: Moses gave their ancestors manna every day for forty years, so surely the Messiah should match that.
Jesus corrects them on two points: it was God, not Moses, who gave the manna; and the Father is now giving the true, lasting bread from heaven.
God’s bread is not a substance but a person — the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the whole world.
Like the Samaritan woman asking for living water, they ask for this bread always — still thinking of something physical.
Jesus makes the first of his great “I am” statements in John: he himself is the bread of life. Coming to him and believing in him satisfies the soul’s deepest hunger and thirst.

f.w: I am the bread of life

n: Jesus reminds them that they have seen him with their own eyes and still refuse to believe. Seeing miracles alone does not produce faith.

f.w: have seen me, and believe not

n: Everyone the Father gives to Jesus will come to him, and Jesus will never turn away anyone who comes. This is one of the most reassuring promises in scripture.

f.w: I will in no wise cast out

n: Jesus describes his entire mission as doing his Father’s will rather than his own — the same submission he will show in Gethsemane.

f.w: not to do mine own will

n: The Father’s will is that Jesus lose none of those entrusted to him and raise them up at the last day. Christ’s care for us reaches all the way to the Resurrection.

f.g: The day of resurrection and judgment at the end of the world.

n: Anyone who truly sees the Son for who he is and believes in him will have eternal life, and Jesus will raise them in the Resurrection.
The listeners grumble, much as Israel grumbled against Moses over food in the wilderness.

f.g: murmur = grumble or complain under the breath.

n: They object that they know his family: how can the son of Joseph, a local man, claim to have come down from heaven? Familiarity blinds them.
Jesus tells them to stop grumbling among themselves.

f.g: A gentle rebuke — complaining shuts out the very teaching that could help them.

n: No one comes to Christ unless the Father draws them. God takes the first step, reaching for every heart; those who respond will be raised up at the last day.

f.w: except the Father which hath sent me draw him
f.g: The JST stresses that a person comes to Christ by doing the will of the Father and receiving the Son.

n: Jesus quotes Isaiah: in the messianic age all will be taught by God. Anyone who truly listens to the Father will recognize the Son and come to him.

f.w: they shall be all taught of God

n: Being taught by the Father doesn’t mean everyone has seen him. Only the one who comes from God — Jesus — has truly seen the Father and can reveal him.

f.g: The JST of John 1:18 adds that no one has seen God “except he hath borne record of the Son.”

n: With a solemn “truly, truly,” Jesus states plainly: whoever believes in him has eternal life — present tense. It begins now.
Jesus repeats the heart of his message in five words.

f.w: I am that bread of life

n: The manna kept their ancestors alive for a time, but those people still died. Even miraculous earthly bread cannot conquer death.
By contrast, the bread from heaven Jesus offers is meant to be eaten so a person never dies spiritually.
Jesus now calls himself the “living bread” and makes the meaning explicit: the bread is his flesh, which he will give up in death so the world can live. Here the sermon turns toward his Atonement.

f.w: my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world

n: The audience argues sharply among themselves, taking his words literally: how could anyone eat his flesh?

f.g: strove = argued heatedly, quarreled.

n: Rather than softening his words, Jesus intensifies them: unless we eat his flesh and drink his blood we have no life in us. He means taking his atoning sacrifice fully into our lives.

f.g: Jewish law forbade drinking blood (Leviticus 17:10-14), which made this saying deeply shocking.

n: Whoever feeds on Christ in this way — by faith, covenant, and continual dependence on him — has eternal life and will be raised at the last day.

f.g: The Greek verb here (trōgō) is vivid — “to chew” — stressing real, personal partaking.

n: His flesh is real food and his blood real drink: only Christ truly nourishes the spirit.

f.g: indeed = truly, genuinely.

n: Partaking of Christ creates a living union: he dwells in us and we in him. The sacrament renews that relationship each week.

f.w: dwelleth in me, and I in him

n: Just as Jesus draws his life from the living Father, those who “feed” on Jesus draw their life from him. Life flows from the Father, through the Son, to us.
Jesus sums up: he is the bread from heaven, unlike manna that could not prevent death. Whoever feeds on him will live forever.
John notes the setting: this sermon was given in the synagogue at Capernaum, where the remains of a later stone synagogue can still be seen today.

f.g: A synagogue was a local Jewish meeting house for prayer and reading the scriptures.

n: Many of his own followers find the teaching too hard to accept. Here “hard” means offensive or unacceptable, not merely difficult to understand.

f.g: Greek sklēros — harsh, hard to stomach.

n: Knowing their grumbling, Jesus asks whether this teaching makes them stumble.

f.g: offend = cause to stumble or fall away (Greek skandalizō).

n: If his coming down from heaven offends them, what will they think when they see him go back up to where he was before? Jesus points ahead to his ascension.

f.w: ascend up where he was before

n: Jesus clarifies that he is not speaking of physically eating flesh. It is the Spirit that gives life; his words are spirit and life to those who receive them.

f.g: quicken = make alive.

f.w: they are spirit, and they are life

n: Still, some of them do not believe. John adds that Jesus knew from the beginning who would not believe and who would betray him.
This is why, Jesus says, no one can come to him unless it is granted by the Father — coming to Christ is both an invitation from God and a choice we make.

f.w: given unto him of my Father

n: A sad turning point: many disciples stop following him. Popularity based on bread could not survive a call to deeper discipleship.
Jesus turns to the Twelve and asks, perhaps with sorrow, if they want to leave too. He never forces anyone to stay.

f.g: In Greek the question is phrased in a way that expects “no” for an answer.

n: Peter answers for the Twelve with one of scripture’s great testimonies: there is nowhere else to go, because only Jesus has the words that lead to eternal life.
Peter adds that they believe and know Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Many manuscripts read “the Holy One of God.”

f.g: Faith first, then sure knowledge — the order Alma describes.

n: Jesus replies that he chose all twelve of them, yet one is “a devil” — an adversary working against him.

f.g: Greek diabolos — slanderer or adversary. Judas would side with Satan’s purposes.

n: John identifies the one Jesus meant: Judas Iscariot, son of Simon, one of the very Twelve, who would later betray him.

f.g: “Iscariot” may mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea.
